## The idea

Not every feedback reinforces. Some correct. A parent who gave the last turn to one child gives the next to the other; a party that lost an election puts more effort into the next; a committee that hired from one department looks elsewhere next time. The balancing process is the Polya urn with the feedback reversed: draw a ball, and return it with a ball of the *opposite* colour.

Now an early run of one colour makes the other colour more likely, so imbalances are corrected rather than amplified. Every urn ends up near half and half, regardless of the order of its early draws. Page uses the two urns side by side to separate processes in which history matters (Polya) from those in which it washes out (balancing).

## Formulation

::: {.model-box}
**Setup.** An urn starts with one white and one gray ball. Each period a ball is drawn at random, and it is returned along with one more ball of the *opposite* colour.

**Equation.** After $t$ draws with $w_t$ white draws, the urn holds $t + 2$ balls, of which $1 + (t - w_t)$ are white (one starting ball plus one for each gray draw), so

$$
\Pr(\text{white at } t + 1) = \frac{1 + t - w_t}{t + 2} .
$$

**Result.** The share of white balls converges to $\tfrac12$ in every run, and the outcome is not path dependent: early draws do not affect where the urn ends up.
:::

The correction is strong: the share of white *draws* deviates from one half by much less than in a sequence of fair coin flips, because every excess of one colour raises the odds of the other.

## Interactive model

Twelve balancing urns (teal) and, for comparison, twelve Polya urns (gray), followed for the same number of draws. The balancing urns all converge to 50%; the Polya urns lock in wherever their early draws pushed them.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, sd, C, fmt, pct} from "../js/models.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof draws = Inputs.range([50, 2000], {value: 500, step: 50, label: "Draws"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 29, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
balance = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const run = (balancing, k) => {
    let w = 1, g = 1;
    const path = [{t: 0, share: 0.5, k, kind: balancing ? "Balancing" : "Polya"}];
    for (let t = 1; t <= draws; t++) {
      const white = r() < w / (w + g);
      if (balancing) { if (white) g++; else w++; } else { if (white) w++; else g++; }
      if (t % 5 === 0 || t < 50) path.push({t, share: w / (w + g), k: `${balancing ? "b" : "p"}${k}`, kind: balancing ? "Balancing" : "Polya"});
    }
    return path;
  };
  const paths = [...range(12).flatMap(k => run(false, k)), ...range(12).flatMap(k => run(true, k))];
  const finals = kind => paths.filter(d => d.kind === kind && d.t === draws).map(d => d.share);
  return {paths, bal: finals("Balancing"), pol: finals("Polya")};
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "Balancing Process: share of white balls, balancing versus Polya urns",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: draws. Vertical axis: share of white balls. Teal lines are twelve balancing urns, which converge to one half; gray lines are twelve Polya urns, which settle at scattered values. The summary below the chart states the result in words.",
  height: 280,
  x: {label: "Draws"},
  y: {label: "Share white", domain: [0, 1], tickFormat: "%", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(balance.paths.filter(d => d.kind === "Polya"), {x: "t", y: "share", z: "k", stroke: C.gray, strokeOpacity: 0.7}),
    Plot.line(balance.paths.filter(d => d.kind === "Balancing"), {x: "t", y: "share", z: "k", stroke: C.teal, strokeWidth: 1.6}),
    Plot.ruleY([0.5], {stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "4 3"})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}

Balancing feedback erases the effect of early draws; reinforcing feedback preserves it.`}</div>`

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# Balancing process: add a ball of the opposite colour; urns converge to 1/2.
draws <- 500
set.seed(29)

urn <- function(balancing) {
  w <- 1
  g <- 1
  share <- numeric(draws)
  for (t in 1:draws) {
    white <- runif(1) < w / (w + g)
    if (balancing == white) g <- g + 1 else w <- w + 1
    share[t] <- w / (w + g)
  }
  share
}
bal <- replicate(12, urn(TRUE))
pol <- replicate(12, urn(FALSE))
cat("Final shares, balancing:", round(range(bal[draws, ]), 3), "\n")
cat("Final shares, Polya:    ", round(range(pol[draws, ]), 3), "\n")

matplot(pol,
  type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey70", ylim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Draws", ylab = "Share white"
)
matlines(bal, lty = 1, col = "#148a91")
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2)
```

## Takeaways

::: takeaways
- Negative (balancing) feedback corrects imbalances, so the process converges to the same outcome whatever its history.
- Positive (reinforcing) feedback, as in the Polya urn, makes outcomes depend on the path.
- Asking which kind of feedback dominates tells us whether history will matter.
:::

## Uses

::: uses
- **Explain.** Why some systems, such as alternating party control or rotating leadership, hover around balance.
- **Design.** Build balancing rules (rotation, quotas, alternating turns) into institutions to keep allocations even.
- **Reason.** Distinguish settings where early luck washes out from those where it locks in.
:::
